analogy: A doctor does not wait for you to collapse; she checks your pulse, temperature and blood pressure on every visit, and keeps your file so she can see what changed. Monitoring is that file for your AI service: every request leaves a record (a trace), the numbers are charted over time, and an alarm rings when one goes out of range. Where it breaks: a thermometer reads the same for everyone, but an LLM can sound perfectly healthy while giving wrong answers, so you also need checks of quality, not just of speed and errors.

scale.title: Tracing 2 million LLM requests a day with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions
scale.html:
Facts: OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions are marked Development and now live in a dedicated repo (opentelemetry.io GenAI page, inference spans). An inference span is named {gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model} (e.g. chat claude-sonnet-5-5), with span kind CLIENT. Traffic and sizes below are our assumptions.

  1. What each span carries. Required: gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.provider.name. Then gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens, gen_ai.response.finish_reasons, gen_ai.response.time_to_first_chunk for streams, and gen_ai.prompt.version. Prompt and completion text (gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages) are Opt-In, because they hold user data.
  2. Volume. 2,000,000 requests x 5 spans (gateway, retrieval, model call, tool, guardrail) x about 1.5 KB of attributes = 15 GB a day of metadata.
  3. Content is the expensive part. At about 8 KB of prompt plus answer per request, capturing all of it adds 16 GB a day of sensitive text. Capture 10% at random plus 100% of errors and thumbs-down (say 2% of traffic): 0.12 x 16 GB = about 1.9 GB a day, with redaction before export.
  4. Turn spans into alerts. Page on p95 TTFT and p95 total latency (not the mean), upstream error rate above 2% for 5 minutes, cost per request 30% above its 7-day baseline, and the share of finish_reasons equal to max tokens (answers being cut off).
  5. Online quality. Judge a 1% sample: 20,000 a day x (2,000 in + 100 out on claude-haiku-5-5 at $0.10 / $0.50 per million) = 20,000 x $0.00025 = $5 a day. Trend the pass rate per intent and per prompt version.
  6. Close the loop. Failed judgments and thumbs-down traces get triaged weekly; real failures go into the golden set from Lesson 12.3.

lab.look_for: Open the lab's JSONL trace file. Each line is one span with OpenTelemetry-style fields: span and parent IDs, timing, model, prompt version, token counts and cost. Find the slowest request and walk its parent-child spans to see whether retrieval or generation took the time. Compare field names with the gen_ai.* attributes above; the lab writes local JSONL instead of exporting over OTLP to a collector, so there is no dashboard or alerting.

quiz.q: Under the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, why are gen_ai.input.messages and gen_ai.output.messages Opt-In rather than recorded by default?

options.t: They contain the actual prompts and answers, which can include personal or confidential data and are large, so capturing them is a deliberate privacy and cost decision.
options.why: Token counts, model and timing are safe metadata; full text is user data. You enable it on purpose, usually sampled and redacted.

options.t: Because OpenTelemetry cannot store strings.
options.why: Span attributes can be strings and structured values; the convention even shows JSON examples for these attributes.

options.t: Because the text is useless for debugging.
options.why: Text is very useful for debugging bad answers. That is why you capture a sample, not none.

options.t: Because providers forbid logging prompts.
options.why: The choice is yours and your users'; the convention makes it explicit so teams decide with privacy in mind.

quiz.q: Mean latency is steady at 3 s but complaints rise. p95 went from 6 s to 19 s. What should you look at first in the traces?

options.t: The slow requests' span trees, grouped by model, prompt version, input token count and tool calls, to see which step and which kind of request got slow.
options.why: Tails usually come from a subset: long prompts, one tool timing out, retries, or one region. Traces show where time went for exactly those requests.

options.t: The overall average token count.
options.why: An average hides the tail just like mean latency does.

options.t: Nothing, the mean is fine so users are wrong.
options.why: Users feel the tail. A 19 s p95 means 1 in 20 requests is very slow.

options.t: The model's temperature setting.
options.why: Sampling settings do not explain a latency tail.

exercises.q: Write the attribute set you would put on one model-call span for a RAG answer, using the GenAI conventions, and give example values.
exercises.a: Span name 'chat claude-sonnet-5-5', kind CLIENT. gen_ai.operation.name='chat', gen_ai.provider.name='anthropic', gen_ai.request.model='claude-sonnet-5-5', gen_ai.response.model as returned, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens=7500, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens=6000, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens=250, gen_ai.response.finish_reasons=['end_turn'], gen_ai.prompt.name='support_answer', gen_ai.prompt.version='v14'. Plus your own app attributes like tenant and request ID. Message content only if opted in and redacted.

exercises.q: Design three alerts for an LLM service and, for each, say what a page should prompt the on-call engineer to check first.
exercises.a: 1) p95 TTFT above 4 s for 10 minutes: check upstream provider status and rate-limit errors, then prompt token counts (did context grow?), then queueing in your own service. 2) Cost per request 30% above the 7-day baseline for an hour: check token counts by prompt version and feature, cache_read share (did prompt caching break?), and agent step counts (a loop?). 3) Online judge pass rate down 5 points on any intent over a day: check prompt or model version changes, index refresh time, and sample the failing traces. Each alert names a first action so the page is actionable.

exercises.q: You run a 5% canary of prompt v15 against v14. After a day, v14 has 9,500 judged samples at 91.0% pass, v15 judged 500 samples at 89.4% pass. Should you roll out v15?
exercises.a: Not yet. The difference is 1.6 points. The SE of v15's rate is sqrt(0.894 x 0.106 / 500) = 0.0138, so its 95% interval is about 86.7% to 92.1%, which includes 91.0%. The data cannot tell them apart. Options: keep the canary running until v15 has a few thousand samples, raise the canary share, or compare per intent where the effect may be concentrated. Also check cost and latency per version from the same traces. Decide the rollout rule (e.g. no intent worse by more than 2 points with 95% confidence) before looking, so you are not choosing after the fact.

interview.q: What would you log for every LLM request in production?
interview.a: A trace with a request ID, timestamps and duration for each step (retrieval, model call, tools), the model ID requested and returned, prompt name and version, input, cached and output token counts, the cost, the finish reason, and any error or guardrail verdict. I would follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute names so tools can read it. Full prompt and answer text is sensitive, so I would capture it only for a sample and for failures, with personal data redacted. User feedback like thumbs-down gets attached to the same request ID.

interview.q: Offline evals pass, but production quality is dropping. How do you find out why?
interview.a: Offline evals only cover cases we thought of. I would check online signals first: judge pass rate on sampled traffic, thumbs-down and re-ask rates, broken down by intent, prompt version, model and tenant. Then I compare traffic mix this week versus last: new topics or languages show up as new intent clusters. I check data freshness, since an index refresh or a stale source changes retrieval. I read a sample of failing traces end to end to see whether retrieval or generation went wrong. Whatever I find becomes new golden-set cases.

interview.q: Design an LLM observability stack for a company with strict data-privacy rules.
interview.a: Instrument with OpenTelemetry using the GenAI conventions so we are not locked into one vendor, and export over OTLP to a collector we run. Metadata such as tokens, latency, model, prompt version and cost is collected for every request. Content capture is opt-in per feature, sampled, and passed through a redaction processor in the collector before storage, with short retention and access controls. Online evals run inside our boundary, with a self-hosted judge if needed. Dashboards and alerts are on tails, cost and judged quality per intent. Audit logs record who viewed raw traces. A DPIA (data protection impact assessment) covers what is kept and why.

analogy: Picture cutting a photo into a grid of small square stickers and describing each sticker with a short code. Now the picture is a list of codes, just like a sentence is a list of words, and the model can read both lists together. Where it breaks: when you cut a photo into stickers, tiny details that cross a sticker's edge, like small print, can get lost, which is one reason VLMs misread small text and miscount objects.

scale.title: Pricing photo triage for 80,000 insurance claims a day
scale.html:
Facts from Anthropic vision docs: Claude splits an image into 28 x 28-pixel patches, so it costs ceil(width / 28) x ceil(height / 28) visual tokens. Claude 4.7 and later models use a high-resolution tier: long edge up to 2,576 px and at most 4,784 visual tokens; bigger images are downscaled. Their example: a 1000 x 1000 image is 1,296 tokens. Traffic numbers are our assumptions.

  1. Volume. 80,000 claims a day x 4 phone photos = 320,000 images, each 4032 x 3024 (12 MP).
  2. Sent as-is. 4032 x 3024 is far over the limits, so each is downscaled to the cap: up to 4,784 tokens per photo. 320,000 x 4,784 = 1.53 billion tokens a day. On claude-opus-5-5 at $4 per million input: $6,124 a day, before any text or output.
  3. Resize first. Damage triage does not need 12 MP. Resize to 1092 x 819: ceil(1092/28) = 39, ceil(819/28) = 30, so 1,170 tokens. 320,000 x 1,170 = 374 million tokens, $1,498 a day on Opus 5.5. A 75% cut from one line of Pillow code, and lower latency because uploads are smaller.
  4. Right-size the model. If an eval shows claude-haiku-5-5 (from $0.10 per million input, models overview) meets your triage bar: 374M x $0.10/M = $37 a day.
  5. Where not to downsample. Reading a licence plate or a VIN needs pixels. Crop that region at full resolution and send it as its own image instead of upscaling the whole photo.
  6. Guard the known weaknesses. Ask neutral questions ("list visible damage") rather than leading ones ("how bad is the dent on the door?"), and send high-value or low-confidence claims to a human adjuster.

lab.look_for: No local vision model is installed for this course, so no lab sends an image. The closest lab is the structured-output one, because the production use of a VLM is usually 'image in, validated JSON out'. Watch the parse-failure rate for free-text prompting versus schema-constrained decoding, and the retry-with-error-feedback loop; the same schema and retry would wrap a VLM call. What it does not show: image tokens, resizing, or visual hallucination. To see those, pull a small vision model (the Ollama vision docs use gemma4) if you have the disk, and pass an images list.

quiz.q: Under Claude's documented patch rule, how many visual tokens does a 560 x 280 pixel image cost (it is under every resize limit)?

options.why: Each 28 x 28 patch is one visual token; small images are not resized.

options.t: 156,800, one token per pixel.
options.why: Models work on patches, not pixels. Per-pixel tokens would make every image unaffordable.

options.t: 1, one token per image.
options.why: An image is many tokens; that is why images are expensive in context.

options.t: It depends only on the file size in KB.
options.why: Cost depends on pixel dimensions after any resizing, not on compression. A heavily compressed JPEG of the same size costs the same tokens.

quiz.q: A user uploads a photo of a living room and asks 'what breed is the dog?'. There is no dog. What is the most likely VLM failure and the best mitigation?

options.t: The model may invent a dog and a breed because the question presupposes one; ask a neutral question first ('list the animals you see') and only then ask about them.
options.why: Leading questions push VLMs into visual hallucination. A neutral first pass grounds the follow-up.

options.t: The model will refuse, so nothing can go wrong.
options.why: VLMs often answer confidently instead of refusing, especially when the question assumes the object exists.

options.t: Use a higher resolution so the model can see the dog.
options.why: There is no dog to see. Resolution does not fix a false premise.

options.t: Lower the temperature so the model is more accurate.
options.why: Lower randomness does not remove a false premise, and newer Claude models do not accept a temperature setting anyway.

exercises.q: Compute visual tokens on Claude for a 1456 x 812 screenshot (under the limits), and its input cost per 10,000 screenshots on claude-sonnet-5-5 ($2 per million).
exercises.a: ceil(1456/28) = 52, ceil(812/28) = 29, so 52 x 29 = 1,508 tokens. 10,000 x 1,508 = 15.08M tokens x $2/M = $30.16. Add your text prompt and output on top.

exercises.q: A support-ticket feature attaches full-page browser screenshots (2560 x 1440) and asks the VLM what error the user sees. Costs are high and the model sometimes reads the wrong error from a sidebar. Propose two changes.
exercises.a: 1) Crop: detect the dialog or main content region (or ask the user to crop) and send only that, which cuts tokens and removes distracting sidebars that cause wrong reads. 2) Combine with text: run OCR on the crop and include the extracted text in the prompt, then ask the VLM to answer using both and to quote the error text it relied on. If its quote does not appear in the OCR text, flag the answer. The why: fewer pixels on irrelevant regions means less cost and fewer chances to attend to the wrong thing, and OCR gives an exact-text check.

exercises.q: Design an eval for a VLM that counts items on retail shelf photos. What metrics and slices, and how do you decide whether it is good enough to replace manual counts?
exercises.a: Golden set: a few hundred shelf photos with human counts per product, covering lighting, angle, occlusion and crowded shelves. Metrics: mean absolute error per product, the share of counts within +/-1, and the share with large errors (off by 5 or more), because a few big misses drive stock-outs. Slice by number of items (VLMs degrade as counts rise), occlusion and image quality. Compare with the current manual process's own error rate, measured on the same photos. Decide in advance: e.g. replace manual counts only for shelves with 10 or fewer items where the error is within +/-1 at least 95% of the time, and keep humans or a detection model for the rest.

interview.q: How does a vision-language model take an image as input?
interview.a: The image is split into small square patches. A vision encoder, usually a vision transformer, turns each patch into a vector, and a projection layer maps those vectors into the same space as the language model's token embeddings. The resulting image tokens sit in the context window next to the text tokens, and the language model attends over both. That is why images cost tokens: for example Claude counts one visual token per 28 x 28-pixel patch, so a 1000 x 1000 image is 1,296 tokens.

interview.q: When would you use a VLM, and when a classic computer-vision model, for an image task?
interview.a: A VLM is great when the task is open-ended or changes often, the labels are expressed in language, volume is moderate, and a few seconds of latency is fine: describing damage, answering questions about screenshots, reading a varied form. A classic model, like a trained detector or classifier, wins when the task is fixed and narrow, volume is huge, latency must be milliseconds, or precise localisation and counting matter: defect detection on a production line, counting items. Often the best system uses both: a detector finds regions and a VLM reasons about the crops.

interview.q: How would you control cost and reliability for a VLM feature processing millions of images a month?
interview.a: Cost: resize to the smallest resolution that passes the eval, crop to regions of interest, route easy images to a cheaper model, cache results by image hash, and use batch processing for anything offline. Reliability: schema-constrained outputs with validation and retries, neutral prompts to reduce hallucination, cross-checks such as OCR for exact text, and confidence routing to humans for high-stakes cases. Measure per-slice accuracy on a golden set, monitor online with sampled human review, and track tokens per image because a client sending larger photos silently raises the bill.

analogy: OCR is like a friend who reads out every word on a receipt in order, perfectly, but has no idea which number is the total. A VLM is like a friend who glances at the receipt and says 'the total is 42 dollars', but might misread a digit. You want both friends: one to understand, one to double-check the exact characters. Where it breaks: friends can disagree and both be wrong, so for money you still need a sum check or a human.

scale.title: Extracting fields from 1.2 million invoices a year for an accounts-payable team
scale.html:
Assumptions (ours): 1.2M invoices a year over 250 working days, 2 pages each, rendered at 1000 x 1400 px. Token rule from Anthropic vision docs: ceil(w/28) x ceil(h/28). Prices: claude-sonnet-5-5 $2 / $10 per million (models overview); Batch API 50% off (batch docs).

  1. Daily volume. 1,200,000 / 250 = 4,800 invoices a day.
  2. Tokens per invoice. Per page: ceil(1000/28) x ceil(1400/28) = 36 x 50 = 1,800 tokens. Two pages: 3,600. Add a 600-token instruction and schema: 4,200 input. Output JSON with line items: 300 tokens.
  3. Model cost. 4,200 x $2/M + 300 x $10/M = $0.0084 + $0.003 = $0.0114 an invoice. 4,800 x $0.0114 = $54.72 a day, $13,680 a year. Invoices are not interactive, so batch them overnight: $6,840 a year.
  4. Checks before payment. (a) Schema validation, (b) the sum of line items plus tax equals the total, (c) OCR digits agree with the VLM on total and bank account, (d) vendor exists in the vendor master. Anything failing goes to a person.
  5. The real cost is people. If 6% fail a check (assumption): 288 reviews a day x 1.5 minutes = 7.2 hours, about one full-time reviewer, which costs more than the model. Cutting the false-flag rate from 6% to 3% saves half a person; cutting tokens by 20% saves about $1,400 a year.
  6. Measure field-level accuracy. On a 500-invoice golden set, report accuracy per field and per vendor layout, after normalising (4210 = 4210.00; dates to ISO). A 99% total but 85% due-date score tells you where to work.

lab.look_for: No local vision model is installed for this course, so no lab sends an image. This lab is the second half of document AI: messy text in, a Pydantic schema passed to Ollama as format, validation, and retry with the validation error fed back. Compare the parse-failure rate of free-text prompting against constrained decoding over the batch of messy emails; invoice extraction fails in the same ways. It does not do OCR or read images. To try OCR locally, Tesseract is free, and its output text can be fed into this lab's pipeline as the 'email'.

quiz.q: An extractor returns valid JSON: total 1,240.00, and line items that sum to 1,420.00. Schema validation passes. What should happen?

options.t: Flag it for review: the arithmetic check failed, so at least one number was misread.
options.why: Valid shape is not correct content. Cross-field checks like sums catch digit swaps that a schema cannot.

options.t: Pay 1,240.00, since the total field is what the schema asked for.
options.why: The two numbers disagree; paying either one without checking risks real money.

options.t: Pay 1,420.00, since line items are more reliable than totals.
options.why: Either could be the misread. You cannot pick one without evidence.

options.t: Retry with a higher temperature until the numbers match.
options.why: Rerolling until numbers agree can produce a consistent but wrong pair. Use an independent check (OCR, human).

exercises.q: How many Claude visual tokens is an A4 page scanned at 150 DPI (1240 x 1754 px)? Is it under the high-resolution tier limits?
exercises.a: ceil(1240/28) = 45 (44.3 rounds up), ceil(1754/28) = 63 (62.6 rounds up), so 45 x 63 = 2,835 tokens. The long edge 1754 is under 2,576 px and 2,835 is under 4,784 tokens, so it is not resized on Claude 4.7+ models. On older standard-tier models (max 1,568 tokens) it would be downscaled, which can make small print harder to read.

exercises.q: Your golden set shows 99.2% accuracy on total, 97% on vendor, but 81% on due_date. List likely causes and fixes.
exercises.a: Causes: date formats differ by country (03/04 is March 4 or April 3), invoices print several dates (issue, delivery, due), and some give terms ('Net 30') instead of a date. Fixes: ask for the raw date string and the format you think it is, then normalise in code using the vendor's country; ask for due_date only when explicitly labelled and otherwise compute it from issue_date plus payment terms; add per-vendor hints for the worst layouts. Re-measure per vendor. The general point: break accuracy down by field, then fix the field-specific cause.

exercises.q: Design the confidence routing for invoice auto-pay so that fewer than 1 in 10,000 paid invoices has a wrong amount, while keeping human review under 5%. What do you need to measure to know you hit it?
exercises.a: Route an invoice to auto-pay only if all independent checks agree: VLM total equals OCR total, line items sum to the total, the amount is within the vendor's historical range, and the bank account matches the vendor master. Everything else goes to review. To prove the 1-in-10,000 target you need a big audited sample: with zero errors observed, the rule of three says you need about 30,000 audited auto-paid invoices to claim the error rate is below 1 in 10,000 at 95% confidence. Measure review rate weekly, and the error rate on a random audit of auto-paid invoices. If review exceeds 5%, find which check fires most and improve that reader, not the threshold.

interview.q: What is the difference between OCR and document AI?
interview.a: OCR turns pixels into text: it finds characters and words and where they are, but it does not know what they mean. Document AI goes further and turns a document into structured fields, like vendor, total and due date, by understanding layout and context. Classic document AI was OCR plus rules per layout. Today a VLM can read the page and return JSON directly. In production you often use both: the VLM for structure and OCR to double-check exact digits.

interview.q: How would you evaluate an invoice extraction system?
interview.a: Build a golden set of real invoices with hand-verified fields, covering many vendors and layouts. Measure exact-match accuracy per field after normalising formats, and break it down by vendor and document quality. Separate errors by cost: a missing field flagged for review is cheap, a confident wrong amount is expensive, so I track the wrong-and-not-flagged rate separately. I also measure review rate and time per review, because that is the operating cost. Every production correction goes back into the golden set.

interview.q: Your company processes 50 document types from thousands of vendors. Would you fine-tune a document model or use a general VLM with prompts? How do you decide?
interview.a: Start with a general VLM plus schemas, because it covers the long tail of layouts with no training and lets us ship and collect labelled data fast. Measure per document type. For the few types with very high volume, a stable layout and accuracy or cost problems, a fine-tuned smaller model or a specialised extractor may beat the general model on cost and latency. The decision is per type, using the eval: accuracy, cost per document, latency and review rate. Corrections from human review are the training data, so the system can move types to cheaper models as evidence accumulates.

analogy: A voice assistant is like a relay race with three runners: the first listens and writes down what you said (speech-to-text), the second thinks of an answer (the LLM), and the third reads it out loud (text-to-speech). If any runner is slow, the whole team is slow, and if the first runner writes down the wrong word, the others carry the mistake to the finish line. Where it breaks: in a real relay each runner waits for the baton, but good voice systems let the runners overlap, starting to speak before the answer is fully written.

scale.title: Call analytics for 20,000 calls a day, and a 1-second voice-agent budget
scale.html:
All volumes, speeds and latencies below are our assumptions or round illustrative numbers; measure your own hardware. Prices: claude-haiku-5-5 from $0.10 / $0.50 per million (models overview).

Part A, batch analytics.

  1. Audio volume. 20,000 calls x 6 minutes = 120,000 minutes = 2,000 hours of audio a day.
  2. Transcription compute. If a Whisper-family model on one GPU runs at 50x real time (illustrative; faster-whisper's benchmarks are a good place to start), that is 2,000 / 50 = 40 GPU-hours a day, about 2 GPUs running around the clock.
  3. LLM cost. 6 minutes x 150 words a minute = 900 words, about 1,200 tokens, plus a 300-token prompt: 1,500 in, 200 out. 1,500 x $0.10/M + 200 x $0.50/M = $0.00025 a call, so 20,000 calls = $5 a day.
  4. Lesson. Here the speech model, not the LLM, is the cost and capacity driver. Optimise STT first: model size, voice activity detection to skip silence, batching.

Part B, real-time agent. Target: reply audio starts within 1.0 s of the user stopping.

  1. Budget. End-of-speech detection 300 ms + final transcript 150 ms + LLM TTFT 350 ms + first clause of 8 tokens at 50 tokens/s = 160 ms + TTS first audio 150 ms = 1,110 ms. Over by 110 ms.
  2. Cuts. Prompt-cache the system prompt to lower TTFT; stream partial transcripts so the LLM starts on the near-final text; start TTS on the first clause, not the full sentence. Shortening end-of-speech detection is the riskiest cut, because it makes the agent interrupt slow speakers.

lab.look_for: No lab processes audio (no speech model is installed). The closest is the generation lab, because the middle stage of every voice pipeline is an LLM call and its TTFT and tokens/sec are the numbers in the latency budget. Note the lab's TTFT and tokens/sec for qwen2.5:7b on your machine, then compute how long the first 8-token clause would take; that is your LLM slice of the budget. If you want the audio halves, faster-whisper and a local TTS install with pip, but they are not part of this course's verified labs.

quiz.q: A meeting-notes product transcribes 1-hour recordings and summarises them overnight. Users complain summaries get names and numbers wrong. Where should you spend effort first?

options.t: Transcription quality: a larger STT model, a vocabulary or prompt with names and jargon, and checking the transcript itself against a few reference recordings.
options.why: The LLM only sees the transcript. Wrong names and numbers usually enter at STT; measure word error rate on a reference set first.

options.t: A bigger LLM for the summary.
options.why: A stronger LLM cannot recover words that were mistranscribed; it will summarise the wrong ones fluently.

options.t: Streaming the summary to the user.
options.why: Latency is not the problem in an overnight batch job; accuracy is.

options.t: A faster TTS voice.
options.why: There is no speech output in this product, and TTS does not affect what the summary says.

exercises.q: A call centre records 3,000 hours of audio a day. If your STT setup processes audio at 30x real time per GPU, how many GPUs run around the clock?
exercises.a: 3,000 / 30 = 100 GPU-hours a day. 100 / 24 = 4.2, so 5 GPUs, with a sixth for headroom and failover. If you can run overnight only (say 10 hours), you need 100 / 10 = 10 GPUs, so the schedule is a capacity lever too.

exercises.q: Design the evaluation for the transcription stage of a call-analytics system in Indian English and Hindi code-mixed speech.
exercises.a: Build a reference set of a few hours of real calls, with human transcripts, covering accents, code-mixing, background noise and phone-line quality. Measure word error rate overall and per slice, plus a targeted metric for what the business needs: accuracy on names, numbers, product terms and Hindi words written in Latin script. Compare two or three model sizes and settings (language hint off vs on, a vocabulary prompt). Then measure the downstream effect: run the LLM classifier on human versus machine transcripts and compare labels. If downstream labels barely change, a cheaper STT model may be fine.

exercises.q: Your voice agent's p50 response start is 0.9 s but p95 is 2.8 s. Name three likely contributors and how you would find out which dominates.
exercises.a: Likely contributors: LLM TTFT tails (provider queueing, long prompts in long calls as history grows), end-of-speech detection waiting on hesitant speakers, and tool calls inserted before the reply (a CRM lookup). To find out, trace every turn with spans per stage (VAD end, STT final, LLM first token, TTS first audio, any tool span) and compare the span breakdown of p95 turns against p50 turns. Whichever stage grows most in the tail is the target: trim history for long calls, speak a filler phrase while a tool runs, or tune VAD per channel.

interview.q: How would you build a free meeting-summary tool from a recording?
interview.a: Record or upload the audio, transcribe it with an open speech-to-text model such as Whisper running locally, then send the transcript to an LLM with a prompt asking for a summary, decisions and action items with owners. If the meeting is long, I would split the transcript into chunks, summarise each, then summarise the summaries. I would show the transcript alongside the summary so users can check names and numbers, because transcription errors flow straight into the summary.

interview.q: What is speaker diarization and when do you need it?
interview.a: Diarization answers 'who spoke when': it splits the audio into segments and assigns each to a speaker label. Plain speech-to-text gives you words but not who said them. You need diarization when the speaker matters: action items with owners in meetings, separating agent from customer in call analytics, or compliance checks on what the agent said. It is a separate model step with its own errors, especially on overlapping speech, so I evaluate it separately, for example by checking speaker labels on a reference set.

interview.q: Would you build a voice agent as STT, then LLM, then TTS, or use an end-to-end speech model? What drives the choice?
interview.a: The pipeline is modular: I can pick the best STT for my languages, any LLM with tools and RAG, and a TTS voice, and I can evaluate and log each stage, including the transcript, which helps compliance and debugging. Its cost is latency and lost prosody, since three hops add delay and the LLM never hears tone. End-to-end speech models cut latency and sound more natural, but are harder to ground, test, guard and audit, and there are fewer choices. For regulated or tool-heavy agents I would start with the pipeline and stream every stage; for casual conversation where latency and naturalness dominate, I would evaluate an end-to-end model.

analogy: Imagine a giant map where every picture and every sentence gets a pin. Pictures of red shoes and the words 'red running shoe' get pinned close together, while 'blue sofa' is pinned far away. To search, you pin your question and look at the nearest pins. Where it breaks: the map has room for the gist, not the fine print, so a pin cannot tell you a shoe's price or model number unless that information is also written in text somewhere.

scale.title: Search over a 2-million-image product catalogue
scale.html:
Facts: the open clip-ViT-B-32 model in sentence-transformers produces 512-dimensional vectors (its config's projection_dim). Image tokens follow the 28 x 28 patch rule in Anthropic vision docs; Batch API 50% off per batch docs. The catalogue size and image sizes are our assumptions.

  1. CLIP index size. 2,000,000 images x 512 dims x 4 bytes (float32) = 4.1 GB; at float16 about 2.0 GB. One CPU machine holds it in RAM.
  2. Caption-then-embed cost. Caption each 800 x 800 product photo with claude-haiku-5-5: ceil(800/28)^2 = 29 x 29 = 841 image tokens + 100 prompt = 941 input, 80 output. 941 x $0.10/M + 80 x $0.50/M = $0.000134 an image. 2M images = $268, or $134 through the Batch API. A one-off cost, re-run only for new or changed products.
  3. Caption index size. MiniLM caption vectors at 384 dims: 2M x 384 x 4 bytes = 3.1 GB.
  4. Query path. Embed the query with CLIP's text encoder and with MiniLM, take top-50 from each index (FAISS or a vector database), fuse with reciprocal rank fusion as in Track 3, then pass the top 5 images plus their captions to a VLM to answer and show the images as citations.
  5. Eval before choosing. 300 real queries with known-correct products. Measure recall@10 for CLIP only, captions only, and fused. Visual queries ("curved velvet sofa") tend to favour CLIP; attribute queries ("walnut, 180 cm, in stock") favour captions and metadata filters. Let the numbers pick the blend.
  6. Scanned documents are different. For page images full of text, models like ColPali embed page patches with a VLM and match query tokens against them, which often beats a single CLIP vector; evaluate it if your corpus is PDFs, not photos.

lab.look_for: No lab embeds images (CLIP and a VLM are not part of the verified local stack). The RAG lab is the same pipeline with text: chunk, embed with MiniLM, search in DuckDB and FAISS, fuse BM25 and vector results with RRF, cite [doc-id]s and refuse below a score threshold. Watch how RRF merges the two ranked lists; in multimodal RAG one list would come from CLIP image vectors and the other from caption text. To try CLIP itself, load the sentence-transformers clip-ViT-B-32 model (check free disk first; it is a separate download).

quiz.q: Users search a furniture catalogue for 'SKU 4471-B oak'. CLIP-only retrieval returns visually similar oak chairs but not the exact product. Why, and what fixes it?

options.t: A CLIP vector captures visual gist, not exact codes; add keyword or metadata search over SKUs and captions and fuse it with CLIP results.
options.why: Exact identifiers need lexical matching. Hybrid retrieval (CLIP plus BM25 or a filter) handles both visual and exact queries.

options.t: CLIP is broken and should be retrained.
options.why: It is doing its job: matching appearance. SKUs are not visual.

options.t: Increase top-k to 1,000.
options.why: The product might not rank in the top 1,000 by visual similarity, and the VLM cannot use that many images anyway.

options.t: Caption every image with a longer description.
options.why: Captions help only if they contain the SKU, which comes from your product database, not from the photo. Metadata search is the direct fix.

exercises.q: How much RAM does a float32 CLIP ViT-B/32 index of 500,000 images need, and how much at int8?
exercises.a: 500,000 x 512 x 4 bytes = 1.02 GB at float32. int8 is 1 byte a dimension: 256 MB (plus small overhead for scales), usually with a small recall loss you should measure.

exercises.q: Your multimodal RAG answers questions about a technical manual with diagrams. The VLM's answer cites a diagram, but engineers say the answer is not supported by it. How do you measure and reduce this?
exercises.a: Measure faithfulness separately from retrieval: for a sample of answers, ask a judge (validated against human labels) whether every claim is supported by the retrieved images and text, and log unsupported claims. Reduce it by asking the VLM to quote or describe the specific diagram element it relied on before answering, sending the diagram at enough resolution to read its labels, including the diagram's caption and nearby text as context, and refusing when retrieval scores are low. Track faithfulness per prompt version so changes are checked.

exercises.q: You must choose between CLIP embeddings and caption-then-embed for a 10-million-photo real-estate archive, and you have budget for only one in year one. Lay out the decision with costs and an experiment.
exercises.a: Costs: CLIP is a local GPU or CPU embedding pass, no per-image API fee; the index is 10M x 512 x 4 bytes = 20.5 GB float32 (10 GB float16). Captioning at the $0.000134 per image computed for 800 x 800 photos is about $1,340 through the normal API or $670 batched, plus a 384-dim caption index of 15.4 GB. Neither is expensive, so the choice is about quality. Experiment: 1,000 photos, 200 real buyer queries ('sunny kitchen with island', '3 bedrooms near park'), recall@10 for each. Visual queries favour CLIP; factual ones (bedrooms, location) belong in structured metadata filters anyway. Pick the one that wins on visual queries, and plan to add the other later as a hybrid.

interview.q: What is CLIP and why is it useful for retrieval?
interview.a: CLIP is a model trained on image-caption pairs so that an image and a matching caption end up close together in the same vector space. It has an image encoder and a text encoder. For retrieval, you embed all your images once, then embed a text query and find the nearest image vectors by cosine similarity. That gives you search by appearance, like 'red running shoe', even when no caption contains those words.

interview.q: Compare CLIP-style shared embeddings with caption-then-embed for multimodal RAG.
interview.a: Shared embeddings match on appearance directly, need no per-image LLM pass, and are cheap to index at scale, but one vector misses fine detail and cannot search non-visual facts. Caption-then-embed turns images into text with a VLM, so it plugs into an existing text RAG stack and can search details the caption spells out; it costs a captioning pass and loses anything the caption omits. Many systems use both and fuse rankings, plus metadata filters for exact attributes. I decide with recall@k on real queries.

interview.q: Design multimodal RAG for 5 million scanned insurance documents with tables, stamps and handwriting.
interview.a: Ingestion: render pages to images, run OCR for text and layout, and use a VLM to extract structured fields and describe stamps, signatures and tables. Index three ways: OCR text with BM25 for exact terms, dense text embeddings for meaning, and page-image embeddings (a ColPali-style late-interaction model) for layout-heavy pages; fuse with RRF and filter by metadata such as policy number and date. Generation: pass the top pages as images plus OCR text to a VLM, require page citations, and refuse on low scores. Evaluate retrieval recall and answer faithfulness per document type, enforce access control at retrieval, and batch the ingestion for cost.
